```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4)
```

This article fits count regressions in which the coefficients differ
between unobserved classes, and in which class membership can depend on
covariates. It covers the two equivalent interfaces, sharing parameters
between classes, choosing the number of classes, class probabilities,
predictions and marginal effects, mixtures of different families, panel
data with one class per panel, diagnostics and inference. Mixtures without
covariates are introduced in
`vignette("finite-mixture-getting-started", package = "flexCountReg")`.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
```

## The model

For unit $i$ with count predictors $x_i$ and membership predictors $z_i$,

$$
P(Y_i = y) = \sum_{k=1}^K \pi_k(z_i)\, f_k(y \mid x_i, \theta_k), \qquad
\pi_k(z_i) = \exp(z_i^\top\gamma_k) \Big/ \sum_h \exp(z_i^\top\gamma_h),
\quad \gamma_K = 0 .
$$

Each class $k$ has its own count regression $f_k$ (any family of
`countreg()`), and the class-membership probabilities follow a
multinomial logit with the last class as reference. Count predictors and
membership predictors play different roles: $x$ changes the expected count
*within* a class, $z$ changes *which class* a unit is likely to belong to.

## Simulated data with two pathways

To keep the two pathways distinguishable, the simulated count predictor `x`
only affects the class means and the binary membership predictor `z` only
affects class membership.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(101)
n <- 600
x <- rnorm(n)
z <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
true_class <- ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(-0.8 + 1.6 * z), 1, 2)
mu <- ifelse(true_class == 1, exp(0.3 + 0.2 * x), exp(1.6 + 0.6 * x))
y <- rnbinom(n, size = 1 / 0.25, mu = mu)
d <- data.frame(y, x, z)
```

Class 1 has low counts and a weak slope; class 2 has higher counts and a
steeper slope. Units with `z = 1` are more likely to be in class 1. Both
classes are NB2 with dispersion $\alpha = 0.25$, i.e. $\ln\alpha = -1.39$.

## Two interfaces, one model

`countreg_lc()` uses latent-class vocabulary (`classes`,
`membership_formula`); `countreg_mix()` uses finite-mixture vocabulary
(`components`, `mixing_formula`). Both call the same estimation engine:

```{r interfaces}
lc <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = d, family = "NB2", classes = 2,
                  membership_formula = ~ z, n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
mx <- countreg_mix(y ~ x, data = d, family = "NB2", components = 2,
                   mixing_formula = ~ z, n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
c(latent_class = logLik(lc), mixture = logLik(mx))
all.equal(coef(lc), coef(mx))
class(lc)
```

Coefficient names are the same in both (`Component<k>:...`); only the
printed labels differ ("Class" or "Component").

## Sharing parameters between classes

By default every class has its own coefficients and dispersion. The
`shared` argument estimates a parameter once for all classes: `dis1 = TRUE`
shares the first distribution parameter (here the NB2 $\ln\alpha$), and
`mean` names formula terms whose coefficients are common.

```{r shared}
lc_sd <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = d, family = "NB2", classes = 2,
                     membership_formula = ~ z,
                     shared = list(dis1 = TRUE), n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
lc_sx <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = d, family = "NB2", classes = 2,
                     membership_formula = ~ z,
                     shared = list(dis1 = TRUE, mean = "x"),
                     n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
data.frame(model = c("class-specific dispersion", "shared dispersion",
                     "shared dispersion and slope"),
           logLik = sapply(list(lc, lc_sd, lc_sx), logLik),
           df = sapply(list(lc, lc_sd, lc_sx), function(m) length(coef(m))),
           AIC = sapply(list(lc, lc_sd, lc_sx), AIC),
           BIC = sapply(list(lc, lc_sd, lc_sx), BIC))
```

Sharing the dispersion costs almost nothing in log-likelihood (the data were
generated with a common $\alpha$), while forcing a common slope is clearly
worse, as it should be. A shared factor is shared as a whole term, never as
individual dummy columns. Distribution parameters can be shared only between
classes of the same family, because the "same" label in two families (e.g.
`ln(alpha)` in NB1 and NB2) does not have the same meaning.

## Reading the summary

```{r summary}
summary(lc_sd)
```

The summary groups the coefficients by class, shared parameters and the
membership model. Below it:

* **Class sizes.** `prior` is the average membership probability from the
  covariates; `posterior` the average posterior probability given the
  outcomes; `effective_n` the sum of posterior probabilities; `modal_n` the
  number of units whose most probable class it is; `mean_count` the class's
  average expected count. Classes are numbered by `mean_count` (a display
  convention: the numbering of same-family classes is arbitrary).
* **Entropy.** How well the posterior probabilities separate the units. The
  relative entropy is 1 for a perfect classification and 0 when every unit
  has probabilities $1/K$. Low entropy does not mean a bad model: the
  mixture can describe the counts well even when individual units cannot be
  classified.
* **Starts** and **observed information** (see
  `vignette("numerical-reliability", package = "flexCountReg")`): how many
  starts reached the selected solution, whether the information matrix is
  positive definite, and the largest gradient component.

The estimates are close to the generating values (class 1: $0.3, 0.2$;
class 2: $1.6, 0.6$; $\ln\alpha = -1.39$; membership $-0.8, 1.6$), with
sampling error. The start table is in `lc_sd$model$starts`.

## How many classes?

```{r choose-k}
lc_1 <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = d, family = "NB2", classes = 1)
lc_3 <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = d, family = "NB2", classes = 3,
                    membership_formula = ~ z,
                    shared = list(dis1 = TRUE), n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
fits <- list(`K = 1` = lc_1, `K = 2` = lc_sd, `K = 3` = lc_3)
data.frame(K = 1:3,
           logLik = sapply(fits, logLik),
           df = sapply(fits, function(m) length(coef(m))),
           AIC = sapply(fits, AIC), BIC = sapply(fits, BIC),
           ICL = sapply(fits, function(m) m$model$ICL),
           starts_reaching_best = sapply(fits, function(m)
             sum(m$model$starts$reached_best)))
```

Here AIC and BIC both prefer two classes, the three-class fit improves the
log-likelihood by about one unit for four more parameters, and ICL prefers
one class. The disagreement is informative: the two generating classes
overlap a lot (the relative entropy in the summary above is below 0.5), so
the mixture describes the counts better than one NB2 regression, but
individual units cannot be assigned to a class with confidence, and ICL
penalizes exactly that. Some caveats apply to any such table:

* No likelihood-ratio test of $K$ against $K + 1$ is reported, and
  `regCompTest()` refuses mixture models: the chi-square reference
  distribution does not hold when a class can vanish or two classes merge.
* ICL ($\text{BIC} + 2 \times \text{entropy}$) favors well-separated
  classes. It answers a classification question, not "which model
  predicts best"; with $K = 1$ it equals BIC.
* Information criteria are comparable only on the same rows and outcome.
  Held-out log scores (see
  `vignette("predictive-validation", package = "flexCountReg")`) are the
  more direct check of predictive value.
* Choosing $K$ from the data and then reporting Wald intervals for the
  chosen model ignores the selection step.

## Class probabilities: prior and posterior

`class_probs()` (or `component_probs()`) returns membership probabilities.
The *prior* probabilities depend only on `z`; the *posterior* probabilities
also use each unit's own outcome.

```{r probs}
prior <- class_probs(lc_sd, conditioning = "prior")
post <- class_probs(lc_sd, conditioning = "posterior")
colnames(prior) <- paste0("prior_", colnames(prior))
colnames(post) <- paste0("posterior_", colnames(post))
head(cbind(d[, c("y", "x", "z")], round(prior, 3), round(post, 3)))
aggregate(cbind(prior_class1 = prior[, 1]) ~ z, data = d, FUN = mean)
table(estimated = max.col(post), generating = true_class)
```

The cross-tabulation is possible only because the data were simulated. The
modal (most probable) class is a descriptive, uncertain classification; it
should not be treated as an observed variable in further analyses without
accounting for that uncertainty.

## Predictions

The expected count of the mixture is the probability-weighted average of the
class expected counts. `predict()` returns either:

```{r predict}
nd <- data.frame(x = c(-1, 0, 1, 0), z = c(0, 0, 0, 1), y = NA)
cbind(nd[, c("x", "z")],
      predict(lc_sd, newdata = nd, type = "component"),
      prior_class1 = class_probs(lc_sd, newdata = nd)[, 1],
      mixture = predict(lc_sd, newdata = nd, type = "response"))
```

The default `conditioning = "prior"` uses only covariates, so these are
predictions for new units; changing the outcome column of `newdata` cannot
change them. `conditioning = "posterior"` gives the retrospective version,
conditioned on the outcomes of units whose counts are known, which is not
an out-of-sample prediction. There is no single linear predictor of the
mixture; `type = "link"` returns one per class.

## Marginal effects: two pathways

A predictor can change the mixture mean through the class means and through
the class probabilities:

$$
\partial m_i / \partial v
= \sum_k \pi_{i,k} \, \partial m_{i,k} / \partial v
+ \sum_k m_{i,k} \, \partial \pi_{i,k} / \partial v .
$$

`margEffTable()` differentiates the full prediction, so both terms are
included, and variables that enter only the membership model (here `z`) are
listed:

```{r margeff}
margEffTable(lc_sd)
```

The effect of `x` works only through the class means; the effect of `z`
works only through membership (moving units towards the low-count class
lowers the expected count). Standard errors use the delta method with the
full covariance matrix of the fit; bootstrap standard errors of marginal
effects are not yet available for mixtures. An overall effect is *not* the
average of the class-specific slopes.

## Mixtures of different families

Classes need not share a family. Here a Poisson class and an NB2 class are
estimated jointly; the names of the `family` vector become class labels:

```{r mixed-families}
mf <- countreg_mix(y ~ x, data = d, family = c(low = "POISSON", high = "NB2"),
                   mixing_formula = ~ z, n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
coef(mf)
mf$model$classes[, c("label", "family", "prior_share", "mean_count")]
c(AIC_mixed = AIC(mf), AIC_NB2_NB2 = AIC(lc_sd))
```

Components of different families keep the order given in `family` (they
are not exchangeable). Only Poisson, NB1 and NB2 are validated as mixture
components; other families can be used, with a message that such mixtures
are experimental.

## Panel data: one class per panel

With `group_var`, every row of a panel belongs to the same unknown class, so
the panel likelihood is a mixture of products,
$\sum_k \pi_k \prod_{t} f_k(y_{t})$, not a product of mixtures. The panel is
the independent unit (BIC uses the number of panels), and membership
variables must be constant within each panel.

```{r panel-data}
set.seed(202)
G <- 120; Tt <- 6
pd <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(G), each = Tt), t = rep(seq_len(Tt), G))
w_panel <- rbinom(G, 1, 0.5)
cls_panel <- ifelse(runif(G) < plogis(-0.5 + 1.5 * w_panel), 1, 2)
pd$w <- w_panel[pd$id]
pd$x <- rnorm(nrow(pd))
pd$y <- rpois(nrow(pd), exp(c(0, 1.2)[cls_panel[pd$id]] + 0.4 * pd$x))
pfit <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = pd, classes = 2, membership_formula = ~ w,
                    group_var = "id", shared = list(mean = "x"),
                    n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
coef(pfit)
c(rows = nobs(pfit), panels = attr(logLik(pfit), "nobs"))
```

### New panels versus panels with a history

For a new panel, only the membership covariates are known, so predictions use
the prior class probabilities. For a panel with earlier observations, the
class probabilities can be updated once with the likelihood of that history,
and then used to predict later rows. Here periods 1 to 4 are the history and
periods 5 and 6 the target:

```{r panel-history}
history <- subset(pd, t <= 4)
target <- subset(pd, t >= 5)
head(history[, c("id", "t", "w", "x", "y")], 4)
head(target[, c("id", "t", "w", "x", "y")], 4)

pred_new <- predict(pfit, newdata = target)                      # prior
pred_hist <- predict(pfit, newdata = target, conditioning = "history",
                     history = history)
head(cbind(target[, c("id", "t", "y")], new_panel = pred_new,
           with_history = pred_hist))
c(MAE_new_panel = mean(abs(target$y - pred_new)),
  MAE_with_history = mean(abs(target$y - pred_hist)))
```

Only the history outcomes are used. Changing the target outcomes does not
change the history-conditioned predictions:

```{r panel-leakage}
target_changed <- target
target_changed$y <- 999
all.equal(pred_hist,
          predict(pfit, newdata = target_changed, conditioning = "history",
                  history = history))
```

Panels without history rows use their prior probabilities. The model assumes
rows are independent given the class; it does not let a panel change class
over time.

## Random parameters within classes

Classes describe discrete groups of units. Units can also differ
continuously within a class: the effect of `x` can vary from panel to panel
around its class mean. `rpar_formula` adds random parameters within the
classes (a latent-class random-parameters model):

$$
L_g = \sum_k \pi_k \int \prod_t f_k(y_t \mid x_t, \beta_k + b)\, dF_k(b).
$$

Each class's coefficient of a random variable is the mean of its random
parameter, and each class has its own standard deviation (`SD:`), unless
`shared = list(rpar = TRUE)` gives all classes the same one. Here the slope
of `x` varies within each class:

```{r lcrp-data}
set.seed(31)
G <- 200; Tt <- 5
rd <- data.frame(id = rep(seq_len(G), each = Tt))
cls <- ifelse(runif(G) < 0.6, 1, 2)[rd$id]
rd$x <- rnorm(nrow(rd))
slope <- c(0.5, -0.3)[cls] + rnorm(G)[rd$id] * c(0.5, 0.3)[cls]
rd$y <- rpois(nrow(rd), exp(c(0.2, 1.5)[cls] + slope * rd$x))
lcrp <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = rd, classes = 2, group_var = "id",
                    rpar_formula = ~ x, rpar_draws = 80, n_starts = 3,
                    seed = 1)
lcfix <- countreg_lc(y ~ x, data = rd, classes = 2, group_var = "id",
                     n_starts = 3, seed = 1)
round(coef(lcrp), 3)
AIC(lcfix, lcrp)
```

The classes are found (true intercepts 0.2 and 1.5, mean slopes 0.5 and
-0.3), and so are the standard deviations of the slope within them (0.5
and 0.3). Without random parameters, the variation of the slopes within
each class is left in the counts, and the fit is much worse.

The likelihood is simulated with `rpar_draws` draws per panel (the same
draws for every class), with analytic gradients. Predictions,
probabilities, class probabilities and residuals integrate over the random
parameters, and `simulate()` draws new coefficients for every panel.
The class expected counts are exact (from the moment generating functions
of the random parameters, as `method = "Exact"` in `countreg_rp()`), and
`Inf` with a warning where they do not exist (a lognormal random parameter
of a positive variable, for example). Conditioning on a panel's outcomes
(`conditioning = "posterior"` or `"history"`) updates its class
probabilities, not its random parameters within the class.
`rpardists` and `correlated` work as in `countreg_rp()`.

Classes and random parameters can stand in for each other: a class can
take the place of a tail of a random parameter, and a large standard
deviation the place of a missing class. Shared standard deviations are
the more stable choice, and the start table shows whether several starts
reach the same solution.

## Diagnostics

Diagnostics use the prior mixture (covariates only), so they do not use each
unit's outcome to classify it before checking it.

```{r diagnostics, fig.height = 3.5}
oldpar <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
rootogram(lc_sd, main = "Two-class NB2")
qr <- residuals(lc_sd, type = "quantile")
qqnorm(qr, main = "Quantile residuals"); qqline(qr)
par(oldpar)
```

Randomized quantile residuals use the mixture's own distribution function;
they are approximately standard normal when the model is correct. A CURE
plot shows cumulative residuals along a covariate:

```{r cure, message = FALSE}
cureplot(lc_sd, indvar = "x")
```

The reference limits drawn by `cureplot()` are those of the cureplots
package, computed from the residuals; treat them as a descriptive guide, not
as a validated band for mixture models. For distribution-only mixtures
(`y ~ 1`) every fitted value is the same, so a CURE plot against the fitted
values carries no information; use rootograms there.

## A real-data example

The bundled `abalone_rings` data hold shell-ring counts of 4,177 abalone
(see `?abalone_rings`). To keep this article fast, we use a random subset of
1,000 animals and a Poisson regression of the rings on the logarithm of the
shell weight.

```{r abalone}
data("abalone_rings")
set.seed(3)
ab <- abalone_rings[sample(nrow(abalone_rings), 1000), ]
ab$log_shell <- log(ab$shell_weight)
ab_1 <- countreg(rings ~ log_shell, data = ab, family = "POISSON",
                 method = "BFGS")
ab_2 <- countreg_lc(rings ~ log_shell, data = ab, family = "POISSON",
                    classes = 2, n_starts = 4, seed = 1)
coef(ab_2)
ab_2$model$classes[, c("label", "prior_share", "mean_count")]
ab_2$model$numerical$information
data.frame(model = c("Poisson", "2-class Poisson"),
           logLik = c(logLik(ab_1), logLik(ab_2)),
           AIC = c(AIC(ab_1), AIC(ab_2)), BIC = c(BIC(ab_1), BIC(ab_2)))
```

Every start reached the same solution, and it is degenerate: the two
classes have practically the same coefficients, the log-likelihood equals
that of the one-class Poisson regression, and the observed information is
singular because the mixing proportion has no effect on the likelihood
when the classes coincide (hence the warning about its standard error).
This is the expected outcome here. A mixture of Poisson distributions is
always at least as dispersed as a Poisson distribution, while ring counts
are underdispersed given shell size (see `?abalone_rings`), so adding
Poisson classes cannot help. The right reading is "no evidence of
classes in this model", not "two groups with about 65% and 35% of the
animals": the reported shares are arbitrary when the classes coincide. For
underdispersed counts, use single-component families that allow it
(`vignette("choosing-a-count-distribution", package = "flexCountReg")`).
When a mixture does improve the fit of real data, interpret its classes
just as cautiously: before reading them as biological groups (for example
infants versus adults), compare them with models that use the observed
`sex` directly.

## Inference

Standard errors come by default from the observed information of the full
parameter vector (all classes, shared parameters and the membership model
jointly), not from the separate EM steps. Alternatives:

```{r inference, eval = FALSE}
# Sandwich standard errors from unit-level (row or panel) scores
fit_rob <- update(lc_sd, stderr = "robust")
# Nonparametric bootstrap of units: each replicate refits the whole mixture
# from the original estimates plus `boot_starts` new starts, and its classes
# are aligned with the original ones before computing the covariance
fit_boot <- update(lc_sd, stderr = "boot", bootstraps = 200,
                   control = lc_control(boot_starts = 3))
fit_boot$model$n_boot_ok        # replicates used
fit_boot$model$n_boot_ambiguous # replicates with ambiguous class matching
```

Near a boundary (a nearly empty class, two nearly identical classes, or
membership coefficients diverging because a covariate separates the
classes) the information matrix is singular or ill-conditioned and Wald
intervals are unreliable; `summary()` reports this under "Observed
information". Overall predictions do not depend on class labels and are
often well determined even when class-specific coefficients are not.

## Not yet available

* Zero-inflated, hurdle and underreporting components within mixtures.
* Different formulas for different components (all components share the
  mean and distribution-parameter formulas, with component-specific
  coefficients unless shared).
* Tolerance intervals for mixture predictions (`tolerance_interval()` refuses
  mixtures). `predict(interval = ...)` gives confidence and prediction
  intervals from the asymptotic normal distribution of the estimates, which
  is poor for weakly separated classes.
* Bootstrap standard errors of marginal effects (`se = "delta"` works).
* A calibrated test of the number of classes.
* Classes that change over time within a panel (hidden Markov models).
* Smooth terms together with random parameters, and heterogeneity in the
  means or variances of the random parameters (`het_mean_formula`,
  `het_var_formula` of `countreg_rp()`).

## Reproducibility

All starts are generated from `seed` and recorded in `fit$model$starts`; the
caller's random-number stream is not changed. The settings, the control
object and the trained model blueprint are stored in the fitted object
(`fit$model$settings`, `fit$model$control`, `fit$model$blueprint`).
